A review of country ambition in targeting important areas for biodiversity under the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework
articles.abstract: Targets 1 and 3 of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF) require actions to focus on areas of importance for biodiversity—a prerequisite for reversing biodiversity loss and halting human‐induced extinctions as set out in the Mission and Goals of the KMGBF. There is a need to review progress on how countries are aiming to identify and conserve such areas of importance. We reviewed 97 national biodiversity strategy and action plans (NBSAPs) and 89 country submissions to the Convention on Biological Diversity's (CBD) Online Reporting Tool (ORT) to assess ambition across five targets of the KMGBF. We searched for evidence that countries were considering where to act for Targets 1, 2, 3, 14, 15, and 21. No country defined what constitutes an important area for biodiversity, and any stated focus of planning was limited largely to existing protected areas or ecosystems. Key Biodiversity Areas were identified in 40% of the NBSAPs, yet only 26% included specific targets, actions, or indicators for these globally significant sites. Ambition toward the 30% restoration (Target 2) and 30% protection (Target 3) targets was higher than previously reported but remained low overall. Only half of the countries planned to mandate or encourage business to measure its impacts on biodiversity (Target 15). Across six measures of ambition, an average of 29% of the countries submitting NBSAPs and 31% of the ORT target countries aimed to meet the KMGBF benchmarks, whereas 48% and 53%, respectively, showed no ambition to do so. European countries showed the lowest level of ambition of any region. Much greater levels of ambition and progress are needed to achieve the targets, goals, and vision for areas of importance for biodiversity in the KMGBF by 2030. Marco conceptual para la aplicación del componente de reducción de amenazas de la medida de Reducción de Amenazas y Restauración de Especies (STAR) Resumen Uno de los objetivos principales del Marco Global de Biodiversidad de Kunming‐Montreal (KMGBF) es detener la extinción de especies y reducir el riesgo de extinción diez veces para 2050. Con el fin de garantizar que las medidas adoptadas en el marco de los objetivos del KMGBF contribuyan a reducir el riesgo de extinción de las especies, se diseñó el indicador «Reducción de amenazas y restauración de especies» (STAR), que permite establecer objetivos basados en la ciencia para las especies. STAR cuantifica la contribución potencial de las medidas de reducción de amenazas o de restauración del hábitat a la reducción del riesgo de extinción de las especies en una zona. Para apoyar la aplicación efectiva de STAR, desarrollamos un marco que permite pasar de determinar el componente de reducción de amenazas de STAR (START) con datos globales a calibrar START utilizando datos locales, para finalmente establecer objetivos y calcular las puntuaciones START reales para medir el progreso. El marco describe los enfoques específicos que pueden aplicarse para calcular estas diferentes métricas START. Primero, las puntuaciones estimadas de START utilizan datos globales para proporcionar una indicación inicial de las especies y las amenazas que se espera que estén presentes en una zona. A continuación, las puntuaciones calibradas de START implican confirmar la presencia local de especies y amenazas y los datos verificados a nivel local permiten establecer objetivos sólidos de mitigación de amenazas que pueden articularse como puntuaciones objetivo de START. El START calibrado también puede servir de base para la gestión reactiva y proactiva de las amenazas. Por último, se supervisan los cambios en la intensidad de las amenazas y se utilizan para calcular el START realizado. Para alcanzar el START realizado, los actores deben no solo reducir las amenazas existentes, sino también evitar que surjan nuevas amenazas en la zona.…

articles.title: Assessing and quantifying variations in the functioning of marine food webs across scales
articles.abstract: The mismatch between the scale of ecological processes and management decisions represents a significant challenge in marine conservation. This misalignment can result in ineffective conservation measures and compromise the sustainability of marine ecosystems. The large spatial resolution commonly used to analyze food webs may obscure key ecological processes and their functioning, leading to inaccurate conclusions with important consequences for management and governance. To address this gap, we used a food web indicator, the survey‐based mean trophic level (MTL), covering an entire bentho‐demersal community across four subregions of the Northeast Atlantic. The indicator was developed at two spatial resolutions, subregional and local (0.2° × 0.2° cells), and we used a long‐term dataset to assess food‐web status. A set of 18 ecological scenarios, based on different trophic level (TL) thresholds and depth ranges, were established for each subregion, and linear models were applied to the historical series for each scenario. At the subregional scale, the results indicated potential recovery of top predators in the northern area; however, the stable patterns under various scenarios may have been attributable to ongoing fishing pressure rather than to true ecosystem stability or a genuinely balanced state. At the finer spatial resolution, local declining trends were revealed that had been masked in the broader‐scale analysis. These contrasting patterns underscore the importance of spatial resolution when assessing the status of marine food webs and highlight the need to consider multiple ecological scenarios. We recommend aligning management strategies with the natural processes that govern marine ecosystems to enhance the resilience and long‐term sustainability of ocean environments. Evaluación y cuantificación de las variaciones en el funcionamiento de las redes tróficas a través de escalas Resumen El desajuste entre la escala de los procesos ecológicos y las decisiones de gestión es un reto importante para la conservación marina. Este desajuste puede dar lugar a medidas de conservación ineficaces y poner en peligro la sostenibilidad de los ecosistemas marinos. La alta resolución espacial que se suele emplear para analizar las redes tróficas puede ocultar procesos ecológicos clave y su funcionamiento, lo que lleva a conclusiones inexactas con importantes consecuencias para la gestión y la gobernanza. Para abordar este vacío, utilizamos un indicador de la red trófica, el nivel trófico medio (NTM) basado en estudios de campo, que abarca toda una comunidad bentónica y demersal en cuatro subregiones del Atlántico nororiental. El indicador se desarrolló en dos resoluciones espaciales, subregional y local (celdas de 0.2° x 0.2°), y con un conjunto de datos a largo plazo para evaluar el estado de las redes tróficas. Establecimos un conjunto de 18 escenarios ecológicos, basados en diferentes umbrales de nivel trófico (NT) y rangos de profundidad para cada subregión y se aplicaron modelos lineales a las series históricas de cada escenario. A escala subregional, los resultados indicaron una posible recuperación de los depredadores superiores en la zona norte; sin embargo, los patrones estables observados en diversos escenarios podrían deberse a la presión pesquera actual, más que a una verdadera estabilidad del ecosistema o a un estado genuinamente equilibrado. A una resolución espacial más detallada, se revelaron tendencias locales de declive que habían quedado ocultas en el análisis a mayor escala. Estos patrones contrastantes subrayan la importancia de la resolución espacial a la hora de evaluar el estado de las redes tróficas marinas y resaltan la necesidad de considerar múltiples escenarios ecológicos. Recomendamos armonizar las estrategias de gestión con los procesos naturales que rigen los ecosistemas marinos para mejorar la resiliencia y la sostenibilidad a largo plazo de los entornos oceánicos.

articles.title: Representation in conservation publishing
articles.abstract: There is a persistent underrepresentation of marginalized voices in academic literature, including that for ecology and conservation. Such exclusion hampers career progression, perpetuating disadvantages for historically marginalized groups in the field, with implications for the direction of conservation research. Diverse perspectives foster novel thinking, strengthen innovation, and ensure research reflects the full spectrum of challenges faced by communities. To assess this underrepresentation, we analyzed self‐reported demographic data for authors of scientific articles to explore demographic trends and how they shifted between 2010 and 2020. The journals chosen were listed as conservation‐related by three or more of the five major journal indices. We used the same dimensions of diversity to assess editor demographics in 2021. In total, 2152 authors and 241 editors completed the survey (response rate: 21.5% authors; 29.5% editors). We found that overall author diversity across multiple traits (Rao's Q) increased between 2010 and 2020. Most notably, the representation of women increased from 29.5% to 35.6% of authors. However, women from lower‐middle‐ or low‐income countries still represented <1% of authors, and most dimensions of diversity saw little change over a decade. In 2020–2021, 80% of authors and 76% of editors self‐identified as White; over three‐quarters of respondents across years lived in high‐income countries; and nationals of three countries (the United Kingdom, the United States, and Australia) represented 34% of authors and 49% of editors (5% of the global population). Our study findings highlight the importance of considering intersectionality, as respondents spanning multiple marginalized identities were disproportionately underrepresented. Overall, our work highlights how a lack of representation continues to characterize academic publishing in conservation and ecology but shows signs of positive change. There is evidence that gender‐based initiatives are having a positive effect, yet more work is needed to enhance representation across other dimensions of diversity. Representación en la literatura sobre conservación Resumen Existe una infrarrepresentación persistente de las voces marginadas en la literatura académica, incluida la dedicada a la ecología y la conservación. Dicha exclusión dificulta el desarrollo profesional y perpetúa las desventajas para los grupos históricamente marginados en este ámbito, lo que tiene implicaciones para la orientación de la investigación en materia de conservación. La diversidad de perspectivas fomenta el pensamiento creador, refuerza la innovación y garantiza que la investigación refleje todo el espectro de retos a los que se enfrentan las comunidades. Para evaluar esta infrarrepresentación, analizamos los datos demográficos facilitados por los propios autores de artículos científicos con el fin de explorar las tendencias demográficas y cómo evolucionaron entre 2010 y 2020. Las revistas seleccionadas figuraban como relacionadas con la conservación en tres o más de los cinco principales índices de revistas. Utilizamos las mismas dimensiones de diversidad para evaluar los datos demográficos de los editores en 2021. En total, 2 152 autores y 241 editores completaron la encuesta (tasa de respuesta: 21,5 % de los autores; 29,5 % de los editores). Observamos que la diversidad general de los autores en múltiples características (Q de Rao) aumentó entre 2010 y 2020. Cabe destacar que la representación de las mujeres aumentó del 29,5 % al 35,6 % del total de autores. Sin embargo, las mujeres de países de renta media‐baja o baja seguían representando menos del 1 % de los autores, y en la mayoría de los aspectos relacionados con la diversidad apenas se observaron cambios a lo largo de la década.…

articles.title: Spatial and Environmental Drivers of Macroinvertebrate Diversity in Groundwater‐Dependent Pan Wetlands Across a Transboundary Aquifer System
articles.abstract: Groundwater‐dependent pan wetlands are keystone habitats for aquatic biodiversity in semi‐arid landscapes, yet the processes that structure their invertebrate communities remain poorly resolved. We surveyed 221 pan wetlands across the Khakhea–Bray Transboundary Aquifer (KBTA), South Africa, a landscape of low relief (1027–1231 m a.s.l.), and asked whether macroinvertebrate assemblages track local physicochemical conditions, landscape position, or both. Pans were assigned to four elevation classes, used here as a surrogate for hydrogeomorphic setting and its hydroperiod consequences rather than as a climatic elevation gradient, because the total relief is an order of magnitude smaller than in studies where elevation acts as a direct driver. Waters were predominantly neutral to alkaline (mean pH 7.6–8.6), consistent with a strong groundwater signature. Dissolved oxygen, water temperature, water depth, ammonium, nitrate and phosphate differed significantly among classes, whereas pH, oxidation–reduction potential, conductivity, total dissolved solids and surface area did not. Assemblage composition differed among classes, but the effect was weak: global ANOSIM detected no separation, and similarity percentage analysis attributed between‐class dissimilarity (67.9%–73.4%) to shifts in the relative abundance of a few dominant taxa, chiefly Anostraca, Spinicaudata and Notostraca, rather than to species turnover. Taxa richness differed significantly among classes, whereas abundance, Simpson, Shannon–Wiener and evenness did not, and within‐class variation exceeded among‐class differences. Shallow, short‐hydroperiod pans were dominated by large branchiopods, whereas deeper, longer‐hydroperiod pans supported proportionally more predatory aquatic insects and molluscs, consistent with hydroperiod and predation, rather than elevation, acting as the operative filters. Boosted regression trees ranked geographic position, particularly longitude, above local physicochemical variables as a correlate of taxa richness; because the surveyed pans are strongly clustered in space, this result is interpreted as evidence of unmeasured, spatially structured habitat variation rather than as a predictive relationship. Conserving these systems will require maintaining groundwater regimes and the full range of hydroperiods across the pan network under coordinated transboundary management, and monitoring assemblage composition rather than richness alone.

articles.title: Urban Habitat Mosaics Structure Gene Flow but Preserve Genetic Diversity in an Invasive Termite
articles.abstract: Urbanization is expanding rapidly in tropical regions, yet its effects on the genetic structure and connectivity of invasive social insects remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how urban and forest habitat contexts are associated with genetic diversity, population structure, and colony organization in the invasive termite Heterotermes tenuis (Hagen, 1858) across three paired urban‐forest sites in Guadeloupe, using 18 newly developed polymorphic microsatellite loci. A total of 414 workers from 50 nests were genotyped. Across habitats, we found no differences in allelic richness, observed heterozygosity, expected heterozygosity, or inbreeding coefficients, suggesting no generalized loss of neutral genetic diversity in urban populations. In contrast, analyses of population structure revealed significant genetic differentiation between urban and forest habitats within each site pair, with habitat explaining 14%–22% of the genetic variation. Isolation by distance was detected in only one site, and a landscape‐level MLPE model indicated that habitat context was a stronger predictor of genetic differentiation than geographic distance. Colony genetic structure was consistent across habitats: no mixed‐family nests were detected, and extended family colonies predominated in both urban and forest environments. Together, these results indicate that urban and forest populations maintain comparable neutral genetic diversity while exhibiting moderate habitat‐associated genetic structuring. However, because habitat type covaried with several environmental characteristics and historical introduction structure cannot be excluded, this differentiation cannot be attributed to urbanization alone. These findings highlight the importance of considering habitat‐associated genetic structure and colony organization when assessing the spread and management of invasive termites in tropical urban landscapes.

articles.title: Whole‐Genome Resequencing Reveals Exceptions to Panmixia in the Exploited Top Fish Predator Antarctic Toothfish (Dissostichus mawsoni)
articles.abstract: Antarctic toothfish (Dissostichus mawsoni) are a critical top fish predator in the Southern Ocean whose population dynamics are strongly influenced by a changing climate and fishing pressure. Their complex, long‐lived life history presents challenges to understanding their population dynamics that we endeavor to overcome through the use of both reduced‐representation sequencing and whole‐genome resequencing data from fish across different cohorts. Our unique sample set allowed us to compare genomic structure, diversity, and demographic changes between cohorts born before and after the year 2000, when changes to fisheries management practices in the Southern Ocean reduced incidences of illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing. While our population structure analyses corroborate recent studies showing panmixia across circumpolar populations of D. mawsoni, comparisons between cohorts revealed key exceptions. A lack of admixture in fish born before 2000 contrasted with widespread admixture among post‐2000 individuals, consistent with increased mixing and/or genotype influx. Notably, genome‐wide diversity declined over time in the Ross Sea (management area 88), with significant losses observed in heterozygosity between pre‐2000 and post‐2000 cohorts. Elevated levels of inbreeding in the Ross Sea, coupled with evidence for recent population contraction from positive Tajima's D values, provided potential explanations for the observed reductions in genomic diversity. Our results reconcile circumpolar panmixia with localized erosion of diversity and elevated inbreeding in the Ross Sea sector, underscoring the value of temporal monitoring and the need to prioritize future research on the interplay between fisheries pressure and environmental change in driving population dynamics and genomic structure in exploited Southern Ocean species like toothfish.

Reconstructing ancient disease ecology through pathogen genomics and palaeoproteomics
articles.abstract: Ancient pathogen genomics and palaeoproteomics have transformed archaeological research on infectious disease by enabling the detection of pathogens, reconstruction of extinct lineages, and investigation of host responses in past populations. Yet pathogen identification alone addresses only part of retrospective diagnosis: whether an individual experienced disease, which tissues were affected, and how infection contributed to morbidity or death. Palaeoproteomics extends this enquiry through the recovery of pathogen proteins, host immune proteins, and tissue-associated molecules from ancient human remains and associated materials. This review evaluates its diagnostic contribution within the broader reconstruction of ancient disease ecology. Dental calculus provides a particularly rich record of oral host–microbe interactions, combining microbial signals with inflammatory and dietary proteins. Studies of mummified skin, muscle and other soft tissues, dental pulp, skeletal lesions, historical bloodstains, coprolites, and latrine residues further extend the range of evidence available for retrospective diagnosis. Protein-based investigations of intestinal infection also illustrate the need to distinguish antibody-based antigen detection from sequence-based proteomics. Published studies support several levels of inference, ranging from tissue identification and inflammatory processes to specific infection and, more cautiously, clinical disease. They also reveal continuing challenges involving peptide specificity, contamination, source attribution, and the interpretation of disease-associated proteins. Retrospective diagnosis is strongest when molecular findings are consistent with anatomical, archaeological, and historical evidence and help discriminate among plausible alternative diagnoses. Protein evidence therefore contributes not only to individual palaeopathological diagnosis but also to broader reconstructions of relationships among infection, diet, sanitation, care, and social conditions. Future progress will depend on comparative samples with and without independently supported pathological evidence, archaeological validation of diagnostic markers, transparent reporting, broader regional coverage, and sampling of finite human remains.

articles.title: Carbon Accumulation in Tropical Dry Forests and Savannas Despite Widespread Land‐Cover Change, Revealed by Radar Remote Sensing
articles.abstract: Accurate mapping of woody biomass and its temporal change is critical for understanding the global carbon balance, informing restoration and supporting evidence‐based policy on climate mitigation and livelihoods. The vegetation of the dry tropics, comprised largely of dry forests and savannas, holds substantial woody carbon stocks, but both stocks and change over time remain uncertain. Where Earth Observation (EO) data have been used to estimate change over time, different products give conflicting results on the direction, magnitude and location of change. We present pan‐dry‐tropical maps of aboveground carbon density (AGCD) and AGCD change at 100 m resolution for the years 2015–2024, developed using ALOS ScanSAR satellite radar observations calibrated with in situ measurements (n = 237). These maps suggest an aboveground woody carbon pool (AGC) in the dry tropics of 25.3 ±$$ \pm $$ 2.0 PgC, ~13.0% of global AGC. Net AGC has increased by 0.43 ±$$ \pm $$ 0.07 PgC yr−1, ~20.0% of the global net land sink. The overall net increase (0.43 PgC yr−1) is comprised of gross losses from deforestation and degradation (0.27 ±$$ \pm $$ 0.05 PgC yr−1) and gains due to densification and extensification of 0.59 ±$$ \pm $$ 0.1 PgC yr−1, with the balance accounted for by small changes (change < 20% of AGCD; 0.11 PgC yr−1). Losses are equally split between degradation and deforestation, while gains are divided roughly 2:1 between the densification of woody ecosystems and expansion into previously grass‐dominated areas. These new maps, created with a dry‐tropics‐specific EO method, highlight the importance of tropical dry forests and savannas in the global carbon cycle. The prominent role of degradation‐related losses suggests that climate change mitigation will need to focus much more on reducing losses from overharvesting than at present. The widespread increases in carbon density and the increase in tree biomass into open systems present major challenges for biodiversity conservation, restoration and livelihoods.

articles.title: Thermal Generalism Shapes Tolerance to Extreme Heatwaves in Estuarine Fishes
articles.abstract: Climate change is widely expected to push many taxa beyond their biological limits, yet some populations persist in environments that routinely experience climatic extremes. This raises a fundamental question: does their thermal tolerance reflect species‐level thermal generalism (an evolved capacity to maintain performance across a broad thermal range) or population‐specific acclimation to local conditions (phenotypic plasticity)? Distinguishing between these alternatives is key for predicting whether tolerance to climatic extremes will generalise across species distributions or remain restricted to heat‐tolerant populations. To test these competing hypotheses, we quantified physiological performance (at cellular and organismal levels) in three economically important estuarine fish (Acanthopagrus australis, Sillago ciliata and Rhabdosargus sarba) collected from 20 sites across 15 estuaries along a ~1000‐km latitudinal gradient spanning their core and poleward range edges. Sites differed in thermal variability, including some that intermittently exceeded the severest end‐of‐century climate projections. We then experimentally exposed two of the fish species from low and high thermal variability sites to moderate (+2°C, 14 days) or extreme (+4°C, 7 days) simulated marine heatwave events, assessing 12 physiological and behavioural proxies. All three species collected in situ maintained comparable physiological performance across sites of contrasting thermal variability. Both experimental species, each collected from a single high‐ and low‐variability site, tolerated heatwave conditions regardless of thermal history or heatwave intensity, supporting species‐level thermal generalism rather than population‐specific acclimation. In the absence of heatwave conditions, S. ciliata from high‐variability sites also showed steeper allometric scaling and faster growth at 26 versus 24°C experimental control temperatures, suggesting this species may benefit from the warmer baseline temperatures projected under gradual climate change. Combined, our findings support thermal generalism as the primary driver of tolerance in estuarine fishes to climatic extremes, with important implications for the fisheries they support under climate change.

Integrated multi-yarn synergistic light-trapping cone evaporator for efficient steam and wire-structured thermoelectric cogeneration
articles.abstract: Facing global freshwater scarcity and energy shortages, this work designs a flower-inspired 3D solar evaporator made from modified ramie yarns that simultaneously generates clean water and electricity. Its conical structure traps sunlight to drive rapid evaporation (1.77 kg m−2 h−1) and produce thermoelectric voltage (38 mV) while resisting salt crystallization even in high-salinity brine, offering a sustainable, off-grid solution for water-electricity cogeneration.

articles.title: A new approach for detecting phenological change using Time of Emergence (ToE) methodology
articles.abstract: Many species are responding to environmental change by shifting the timings of phenological events such as migration or reproduction. These shifts are typically reported as rates of change, which do not indicate when such shifts transcend their original states, nor consider whether species experience novel environmental conditions or phenological mismatch with other species at their phenological events. We present a new, generalizable approach to detect and contextualize shifts in phenological data regardless of taxonomic group or location by applying statistical and empirical Time of Emergence (ToE) metrics derived from climate science. Our approach conclusively identifies when species depart from their baseline phenological event timings and determines whether they experience novel environmental conditions or phenological mismatch with other species during their phenological event. In combination, these metrics detect emergence in timing, environment and community synchrony for species' phenological responses. We explore these metrics using simulations then apply them to a diverse set of example datasets (butterflies, marine plankton and cherry blossoms). We then develop community‐wide indicators of phenological emergence, environmental emergence and species mismatch, which can be applied to inform biodiversity policy at any scale and for any taxa. These methods are available via the phenometrics R package.

articles.title: Estimating absolute DNA abundance from replicated metabarcoding
articles.abstract: Datasets derived from mixed‐template DNA amplification and sequencing (‘metabarcoding’) are common in environmental DNA (eDNA), microbiome or microbial ecology analyses. Such metabarcoding data have been broadly used to inform estimates of biodiversity, distribution and abundance across a wide range of species and habitats. Generally, data from metabarcoding consist of a table of read‐counts assigned to each of a set of taxa or sequence variants. As such, they appear to contain quantitative information about the environment under study, immediately eligible for traditional community ecology analyses. In fact, metabarcoding data are compositional, can be biased by variation in PCR amplification rates among taxa, and have other statistical attributes that are distinct from many other common ecological observations. The difficulty in understanding and accounting for the complexity of metabarcoding observations has hindered their ecological interpretation and limited their integration with other ecological data types. Here, we use both simulations and empirical observations to show that the variability among replicate metabarcoding observations is closely tied to the absolute quantities of DNA present in a sample. We then develop a general statistical model for estimating DNA abundance from metabarcoding observations using the relationship between mean and variance of metabarcoding reads. We demonstrate that the model can effectively estimate DNA abundances using simulations and from experimentally created DNA samples. The model can be applied to a single marker or to multiple markers simultaneously, allowing the direct integration of information from multiple genetic markers derived from a common biological sample. Estimates of absolute DNA abundance are the logical unit to connect DNA observations to organismal abundance or biomass. Our methods can be used to link together multiple types of DNA observations or to connect DNA observations with non‐genetic ecological methods for surveying ecosystems. However, important aspects of the ‘ecology of DNA’ remain unresolved and may limit our ability to link observed concentrations to organismal abundances in a general way.

articles.title: Seeing both the forest and the trees: An automated workflow for ultra‐high‐resolution drone imaging of tropical canopies
articles.abstract: Tropical forest canopies host diverse tree and liana assemblages, yet key foliar and reproductive traits needed for taxonomic identification of canopy plants are often difficult to see from the forest floor, creating a bottleneck in inventories. We introduce a drone-based workflow that automatically acquires hundreds of close-up, ultra-high-resolution photographs (~0.4 mm pixel−1) of selected tree crowns per day, enabling efficient botanical and ecological studies of canopy plants (demo: https://youtu.be/80goMEifpc4). The approach leverages a compact DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise (M3E) with wide-angle and telephoto cameras to (i) generate a high-resolution digital surface model and orthomosaic via structure-from-motion photogrammetry and (ii) capture close-up photographs from ~6 m above the canopy at preplanned locations. Photographs are accurately (<13 cm error) geolocated with real-time kinematic (RTK) global navigation satellite system to support spatial co-registration with photogrammetric products. In field deployments, we acquired close-up photographs for up to ~300 selected canopy trees per day and maintained RTK corrections over operational distances up to ~3 km, illustrating the potential of the method for plot- to landscape-scale studies. The level of visual detail in the close-up photographs of canopy crowns was sufficient to support expert identification in a majority of cases in our tropical forest study sites despite their high taxonomic diversity. Although developed for tropical trees and lianas, the workflow is applicable to other forest and vegetation types for botanical, phenological and ecological applications. We outline strengths and limitations of the workflow to guide use and also provide harpia , an open-source Python library to program automatic close-up missions with the M3E (code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22116831). Resumen El dosel de los bosques tropicales alberga diversas comunidades de árboles y lianas. Sin embargo, las características foliares y reproductivas clave necesarias para la identificación taxonómica de las especies del dosel suelen ser difíciles de observar desde el suelo del bosque, lo que limita el progreso en los inventarios. Presentamos un flujo de trabajo basado en drones que adquiere automáticamente cientos de fotografías de primer plano de ultra alta resolución (~0,4 mm píxel−1) de copas de árboles seleccionadas por día, agilizando los estudios botánicos y ecológicos de las especies del dosel (demostración: https://youtu.be/80goMEifpc4). Utilizamos un dron DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise (M3E) compacto, equipado con cámaras gran angular y teleobjetivo, para (i) generar un modelo digital de superficie y un ortomosaico de alta resolución mediante fotogrametría de estructura a partir del movimiento (structure-from-motion) y (ii) capturar fotografías de primer plano desde ~6 m sobre el dosel en ubicaciones planificadas previamente. Las fotografías se georreferencian con precisión (error <13 cm) mediante un sistema global de navegación por satélite (GNSS) con posicionamiento cinemático en tiempo real (RTK), facilitando su corregistro espacial con los productos fotogramétricos. En campañas de campo, adquirimos fotografías de primer plano de hasta ~300 árboles de dosel diarios y mantuvimos correcciones RTK a distancias operativas de hasta ~3 km, lo que evidencia el potencial del método para estudios desde nivel de parcela hasta paisaje. La alta resolución de las fotografías permitió la identificación taxonómica por expertos en la mayoría de los casos, aun en ecosistemas de bosque tropical con elevada diversidad taxonómica. Aunque se desarrolló para árboles y lianas tropicales, el flujo de trabajo es aplicable a otros tipos de bosques y vegetación con fines botánicos, fenológicos y ecológicos.…

articles.title: TreeSegAgent: Agentic tree instance segmentation via a multi‐anchor pipeline
articles.abstract: Individual‐tree segmentation from three‐dimensional forest point clouds underpins forest inventory, biomass estimation and ecosystem monitoring, but remains challenging in structurally complex stands, where vertical heterogeneity and point‐density degradation weaken the robustness of centre‐offset‐based instance grouping. We present TreeSegAgent, an extensible framework for forest point‐cloud analysis, whose core segmentation component is a multi‐anchor framework for tree segmentation (MA‐TreeSeg). MA‐TreeSeg stabilizes instance formation through two modules. First, a multi‐anchor (three‐vertical‐anchor) structural grouping module within an enhanced PointGroup‐style instance segmentation network, explicitly encoding tree vertical structure to improve grouping stability under sparse canopy conditions and to better recover low‐stature and understory trees. Second, we incorporate segment anything model (SAM)‐driven trunk constraint module. SAM is applied on two‐dimensional projections to identify trunk regions and generate trunk candidates, which are then employed as spatial hard constraints to regularize centre‐offset predictions and suppress clustering drift under canopy overlap. To support reproducible ecological workflow, TreeSegAgent further provides a task‐driven agent for automated, specification‐driven orchestration of common point‐cloud operations (e.g. instance segmentation, DEM generation and height‐based filtering) across datasets. Across multiple forest point‐cloud benchmarks, our method yields more spatially coherent individual‐tree instances and improved robustness to density variation, offering an extensible solution for large‐scale forest point‐cloud analysis.

articles.title: Turning Red to Green Repeatedly: Ancestral LWS Duplications Drive Convergent Visual Tuning in Teleost Fishes
articles.abstract: Photopigments, formed by an opsin protein bound to a light‐sensitive chromophore, underlie vertebrate vision. Long‐wavelength–sensitive (LWS) opsins mediate red‐light detection, and most teleosts retain a single functional LWS1. A shorter‐shifted green‐sensitive paralog (LWS2) is found only in a few lineages. By mining teleost genomes and sequencing retinal transcriptomes, we identify elopomorphs as an additional lineage retaining LWS2 (alongside characins and osteoglossomorphs). Surprisingly, we reveal a previously overlooked, shorter‐shifted paralog, LWS3, restricted to gobies (Percomorpha) and arising from an ancestral duplication either in the teleost or in the percomorph ancestor. Structural modelling of twelve LWS opsins reveals convergent evolution at four key amino acid sites (214, 259, 261, 269) in the retinal‐binding pocket, indicating convergent substitutions in human MWS (an old‐world primate‐specific duplicate of the vertebrate LWS1), teleost LWS2, and goby LWS3 relative to red‐sensitive counterparts, consistent with repeated spectral shifts towards greener wavelengths. In several lineages, including characins, mormyrids, gobies, and primates, these shorter‐shifted LWS opsins have at least partially replaced the canonical green‐sensitive RH2‐based visual pigment. Retinal transcriptomes revealed variable lws3 expression across adult gobies, either complementing lws1 in most species, or dominating the visual opsin expression profile as in the sicydiines. In situ hybridisation in the whitebarred goby (Amblygobius phalaena; Valenciennes, 1837) showed that lws1 and lws3 are expressed in separate double‐cone members, analogous to rh2 expression in other fish species. Together, these results show that repeated convergence towards shorter LWS sensitivity in vertebrate evolution involves coordinated changes at the molecular, regulatory, and functional levels, providing a striking example of multilevel sensory adaptation.

Engineering High-Entropy Tetrahedrite Cu–Zn–Sb–Ag–Bi–S Nanocrystals via Sequential Cation Exchange as Efficient Catalysts for Hydrogen Evolution Reactions
articles.abstract: High-entropy chalcogenides represent an emerging class of functional materials with immense potential in broad applications. To date, colloidal high-entropy nanocrystals (NCs) have predominantly been accessed via co-nucleation of precursors or simultaneous incorporation of multiple cations. While effective, these approaches lack a mechanistic understanding of NC synthesis. Here, we report the colloidal synthesis of high-entropy Cu–Zn–Sb–Ag–Bi–S NCs in the tetrahedrite phase, employing a sequential, low-temperature cation-exchange strategy, starting from a Cu–Zn–Sb–S tetrahedrite template. Subsequent sequential cation exchanges preserve the crystal phase while enabling precise control over morphology. This bottom-up approach circumvents the need for high-temperature synthesis, while allowing isolation and characterization of intermediate states, providing important mechanistic insight into the evolution of high-entropy NCs. The nanocrystals served as hydrogen evolution reaction electrocatalysts with less negative cathodic potentials. This work introduces the high-entropy tetrahedrite phase, paving the way for entropy-stabilized chalcogenides for energy conversion applications.

articles.title: Magnetism beyond the Monolayer: Long-Range Order in an Interfacial Phase of CoBr2
articles.abstract: Transition metal dihalides are promising magnetic van der Waals materials because of their structural simplicity, chemical stability, and compatibility with nanofabrication. While magnetic order in these systems is typically associated with bulk-like monolayers, its relation to interfacial phases remains largely unexplored. Here we show that in CoBr2 grown on Au(111), long-range magnetic order already emerges in a structurally distinct interfacial precursor phase, prior to the formation of the bulk-like monolayer. During growth, this phase evolves into the monolayer, accompanied by a transition from molecular-like states to semiconducting behavior. Spin-resolved STM reveals an inhomogeneous in-plane magnetic response that is locally suppressed by point defects, whereas macroscopic XMCD demonstrates robust long-range order with pronounced in-plane anisotropy. These results establish that long-range magnetic order in CoBr2 does not require an ideal bulk-like monolayer but can emerge from interfacial phases with distinct electronic and structural properties, enabling magnetism beyond the monolayer limit.

articles.title: Nonlinear Optical Fingerprints of Defects in Hexagonal Boron Nitride
articles.abstract: Hexagonal boron nitride (h-BN) defects are promising building blocks for quantum photonics and sensing, yet their nonlinear optical signatures remain poorly understood. We use first-principles calculations to determine the polarization-resolved linear, second-order, and third-order susceptibilities of multilayer h-BN containing vacancies and carbon-based defect complexes. Defects weakly affect the linear response but strongly enhance nonlinear susceptibilities through symmetry breaking and resonant defect transitions. Carbon complexes produce orders-of-magnitude increases in second-harmonic generation and distinct polarization-dependent spectra that differentiate defects with identical composition but different geometry. Third-harmonic generation is also enhanced, although it is less sensitive to local structure. Measurements on carbon-doped h-BN qualitatively support these trends. These results establish nonlinear spectroscopy as a powerful probe of defect identity and geometry in h-BN and provide a route to defect-engineered nonlinear quantum photonics.

articles.title: Physics-Consistent Generative Hologram Design for Multifocal Femtosecond Laser Fabrication
articles.abstract: Multifocal phase holography offers a route to parallel femtosecond laser micro- and nanofabrication, but conventional weighted Gerchberg–Saxton (GSW) phase retrieval requires target-specific iterations and does not jointly optimize the optical quantities governing exposure quality. Here we introduce PhyFlow, a physics-consistent invertible flow model that generates phase-only multifocal holograms from target multifocal patterns in a single inverse pass. A multiscale invertible backbone learns target-to-phase correspondence, while differentiable Fourier optics constraints optimize diffraction efficiency, focal uniformity, and target-shape preservation. Across focal numbers and array scales, PhyFlow matches or surpasses GSW in energy concentration, focal balance, and shape fidelity while reducing per-hologram generation time by 98.8%. Optical-field measurements and femtosecond laser writing further show improved dot-area consistency, narrower line width distributions, and fewer nontarget written features. PhyFlow therefore connects rapid learned hologram generation with physically optimized fields and more uniform parallel fabrication.

articles.title: Precursor-Free Photoelectrochemical Fabrication of Spiral Lead Oxide Nanostructures under Circularly Polarized Light
articles.abstract: Chiral nanostructures have attracted considerable attention because of their strong interactions with circularly polarized light (CPL) and their various applications. Although various fabrication methods have been reported, photoelectrochemical approaches using CPL as the chiral source are attractive because of their simplicity, cost-effectiveness, and scalability. However, previous CPL-based methods have required two or more steps, including the preparation of anisotropic precursors. Here, we demonstrate a single-step method for the selective growth of chiral PbO2 nanostructures with handedness dictated by CPL at a chiral yield of 87%, by simply irradiating a transparent electrode with CPL, without using precursor nanoparticles. The obtained structures exhibit well-defined spiral morphologies and high chiroptical activity with maximum dissymmetry factors (g-factors) ranging from 0.006 to 0.010. This conceptual framework, involving symmetry breaking through random nucleation and Mie-resonance-mediated spiral growth under CPL, may be applicable to the template-free fabrication of various chiral nanomaterials.

articles.title: Pressure Engineering through Silica Nanoconfinement for Melting Point Elevation of Gold Nanoparticles
articles.abstract: Au nanoparticles (NPs) are inherently thermally unstable at elevated temperatures because their large surface-to-volume ratio promotes melting, migration, and coalescence. Here, we demonstrate that silica (SiO2) nanoconfinement thermodynamically elevates the melting point (Tm) of Au NPs through confinement-induced compressive pressure. Atomic-resolution in situ heating scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) combined with local Fourier crystallinity mapping reveals that bare Au NPs lose crystallinity at 1,000 °C, whereas SiO2-encapsulated Au cores (Au@SiO2) remain crystalline. Accordingly, in situ heating TEM shows bare Au NPs progressively merge while Au@SiO2 remain structurally isolated. Temperature-dependent lattice-parameter measurements reveal significantly suppressed thermal expansion of confined Au cores, corresponding to an estimated compressive stress of 4–5 GPa. Finite-element simulations support this estimate, showing that SiO2 shell shrinkage generates several-GPa core pressure, with thicker shells producing higher pressure and greater Tm elevation. These findings establish nanoconfinement-induced pressure as a general thermomechanical strategy for stabilizing metallic NPs under extreme thermal environments.

articles.title: Squaring the Hexagon: Multiply Twinned Plasmonic Magnesium Nanocubes
articles.abstract: Magnesium, a promising alternative for sustainable nanophotonics, crystallizes in a hexagonal close-packed (HCP) system, unlike the face-centered cubic (FCC) structures of gold, silver, copper, and aluminum. We report the high-yield colloidal synthesis of an unexpected shape in an HCP system: cubes. Nanocubes with narrow size distributions were produced from colloidal reduction of a magnesium precursor in the presence of a sodium salt nucleating agent. Electron microscopy and diffraction reveal multiple twinning leading to the formation of six single-crystal units within the nanocubes. A self-limiting, sub-10 nm passivating oxide layer protects the metallic core against further oxidation in air and organic solvents. Strong, multimode plasmonic responses were observed using bulk extinction spectroscopy, single-particle scattering correlated with electron microscopy, and electron energy loss spectroscopy; experimental results were corroborated by numerical simulations. These findings expand the crystallographic boundaries of non-FCC plasmonics and establish magnesium nanocubes as versatile building blocks for nanophotonic applications.

articles.title: Termination-Dependent Surface Fermiology in the Intercalated Altermagnet CoNb4Se8
articles.abstract: Altermagnets have recently gained attention for hosting symmetry-enforced spin-split bands despite zero net magnetization. Angle-resolved photoelectron spectroscopy (ARPES) offers direct access to their electronic structure. However, the intrinsic surface sensitivity of this technique complicates the identification of the observed features: Surface states can be misinterpreted as the spin-split counterpart of bulk bands. This issue becomes particularly relevant for layered intercalated systems, where micrometer-sized domains with distinct terminations often coexist on a cleaved surface. We discuss this scenario for CoNb4Se8, one of the first established layered altermagnets. Supported by density functional theory calculations, we employ micro-ARPES to probe individual domains and reveal two contrasting surface terminations. We identify Co- and Se-terminated domains with characteristic surface states arising from bulk-surface connectivity of the material. Our work shows that termination-dependent surface contributions are essential for the reliable spectroscopic identification of altermagnetism and for assessing its presence across the family of layered materials.

articles.title: Ultrathin BiO x Charge-Transfer Doping for Cross-TMD Electronic Modulation and Homogeneous WSe2 Inverters
articles.abstract: Charge-transfer doping provides a nondestructive route to tune two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), but selectively patterned n-type dopants effective across different TMD channels remain limited. Here, ultrathin bismuth oxide (BiOx) is used as an n-type charge-transfer doping and passivation layer for monolayer MoS2 and WSe2 transistors. In MoS2, 2 nm BiOx preserves the channel structure and yields a TLM-extracted effective contact resistance of 0.71 ± 0.06 kΩ·μm at n2D = 1.8 × 1013 cm–2. Thicker BiOx strengthens n-type modulation but reduces gate controllability. The modulation remains stable after ambient storage and air annealing. BiOx also enhances electron transport in WSe2 and enables homogeneous WSe2 inverters with MoOx-doped p-FETs, achieving a gain of ∼19 and a total normalized noise margin of 0.895 VDD at VDD = 2 V. These results establish BiOx as a cross-TMD n-type charge-transfer dopant for contact, threshold-voltage, and polarity engineering.

articles.title: Spatiotemporal remodeling in habenula marks the onset of depression-related phenotypes
articles.abstract: Chronic stress has lasting adverse consequences that can lead, over time, to depression, yet the optimal timeframe for effective therapies remains unclear. The lateral habenula (LHb) has been implicated in stress-related behavioral repercussions, but the precise timing of its contribution is not understood. Here, using spatial transcriptomics, we generated a spatially resolved molecular atlas of the LHb of male mice, revealing a topographically organized and temporally defined remodeling of gene expression after chronic stress. Longitudinal in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of individual LHb neurons revealed progressively heightened excitatory responses to aversive stimuli. These neuronal adaptations mirrored both the progression of transcriptional changes and the emergence of depression-related behavioral phenotypes and were reversed by the antidepressant ketamine. Moreover, chemogenetically limiting LHb neuronal activity or administering ketamine at the onset of these changes exerted antidepressant effects. These findings link spatiotemporal signatures of LHb neuronal ensembles and genetic landscape with the onset of stress-induced depression-related states.

articles.title: Contrasting CH4 flux responses to distinct drought regimes and nitrogen enrichment in a temperate steppe
articles.abstract: Grassland CH4 sink stability is governed by divergent pathways under distinct drought regimes. While intense drought triggers transient inhibition via legacy effects on belowground productivity (BNPPlag), chronic drought and reduced rainfall frequency exert persistent suppression through coupled biotic‐abiotic shifts. Notably, Artemisia frigida expansion stimulates biogenic methane emissions, significantly offsetting soil CH4 oxidation. This suppression is reinforced by diminished arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal (AMF) abundance and altered nutrient availability, whereas nitrogen addition acts as a functional buffer under specific scenarios. Summary Drought and nitrogen (N) deposition alter greenhouse gas fluxes, but how distinct drought scenarios interact with N enrichment to regulate the methane (CH4) sink remains poorly understood. We conducted a 4‐yr field experiment in a temperate steppe to examine CH4 fluxes under three drought regimes – early‐season intense drought (ID), mid‐season chronic drought (CD), and mid‐season reduced rainfall frequency (RF) – and N addition. CH4 uptake and its driving mechanisms were assessed through field measurements and structural equation modeling, focusing on the interplay between soil physicochemical properties, microbial abundance, and plant‐mediated emissions. All drought treatments reduced the CH4 sink with divergent temporal dynamics; reduced RF caused the most persistent reduction, while N addition alleviated the inhibitory effects of CD. These shifts were driven by distinct mechanisms: ID acted via lowering previous‐year belowground net primary productivity and increasing dissolved organic N, CD functioned through increased Artemisia frigida cover and reduced arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal abundance, and RF suppressed uptake via the morphological expansion of A. frigida. We conclude that CH4 sink stability is highly sensitive to drought regime, and that the morphological expansion of specific plants such as A. frigida may partially offset the soil CH4 sink.

articles.title: Evolutionary shifts to gynomonoecy correlate with changes in capitulum architecture in South African Helichrysum (Asteraceae)
articles.abstract: Representative South African Helichrysum species illustrating variation in capitulum size. Summary Gynomonoecy has evolved repeatedly in Asteraceae, suggesting selective advantages for species whose capitula combine pistillate and bisexual flowers. Theories invoking conspicuous peripheral flowers and achene heteromorphism do not account for gynomonoecy in the southern African‐centred genus Helichrysum, which lacks both these features. We investigated whether gynomonoecy is associated with changes in capitulum architecture in South African Helichrysum, focusing on flower packing density and achene size. We compared flower packing density and achene size between hermaphroditic and gynomonoecious Helichrysum species using phylogenetic generalised least squares and reconstructed ancestral sexual systems using a well‐sampled, time‐calibrated phylogeny. Gynomonoecious species produced nearly twice as many flowers per unit receptacle area as hermaphroditic species and had subtly but significantly smaller achenes. Ancestral‐state reconstruction strongly supported hermaphroditism as ancestral, with gynomonoecy originating independently 18 times. Our results provide the first phylogenetically informed evidence within a single Asteraceae genus that shifts to gynomonoecy correlate with shifts in capitulum architecture. The association between gynomonoecy, denser flower packing, and reduced achene size is consistent with the hypothesis that accentuated resource gradients within capitula and priority access to resources by first‐maturing peripheral flowers may have favoured the evolution of gynomonoecy.

articles.title: MAIT cells in gastrointestinal cancer: immunity to therapy
articles.abstract: Mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells are emerging as important regulators of immunity in gastrointestinal (GI) cancers. Enriched in mucosal and hepatic tissues, MAIT cells recognize microbial-derived metabolites presented by MHC class I-related molecule MR1 and rapidly exert effector functions, including cytokine production and cytotoxicity. Across GI malignancies, including hepatocellular carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, colorectal, gastric, pancreatic, and esophageal cancers, MAIT cells display context-dependent roles shaped by the tumor microenvironment, microbiome, and immune signaling pathways. While they can mediate antitumor immunity, they frequently exhibit functional exhaustion or adopt pro-tumorigenic phenotypes. Therapeutic strategies aim to enhance MAIT cell activity, reverse dysfunction, and integrate them into combinatorial immunotherapy approaches. Understanding MAIT cell biology may enable their exploitation as biomarkers and therapeutic targets in GI cancers.

articles.title: Advances in poly(disulfide)s: dynamic polymerization of cyclic disulfides
articles.abstract: Advances in dynamic covalent chemistry have dramatically broadened its use in polymer research. Cyclic disulfide bonds are a widely used, versatile platform for engineering dynamic polymers. The resulting polymers leverage the dynamic character of exocyclic linkages associated with cyclic disulfide bonds, along with modular, tailorable chain-end functionalities to enable self-healing and chemical recycling. This review summarizes recent advances in dynamic polymer chemistry based on cyclic disulfide bonds that have enabled new design principles for the development and innovation in advanced polymers. We highlight living/controlled polymerization strategies for cyclic disulfide monomers, covering the principal polymerization strategies and mechanisms, and discuss the future challenges and prospective directions of the field in the context of emerging societal and technological demands.

articles.title: Plant reproductive palaeobiology: a window into long-term reproductive dynamics
articles.abstract: Reproductive dynamics strongly influence genetic diversity and population structure, with important implications for ecological interactions and evolutionary trajectories. However, our understanding of plant reproductive dynamics remains limited due to the scarcity of long-term studies. Here, we propose a conceptual and methodological framework for tracking plant reproductive dynamics over long timescales using pollen, plant spore, and seed records preserved in sedimentary archives. The analysis of counts, morphology, and DNA from fossil propagules enables reconstruction of reproductive patterns over centennial to million-year timescales. When integrated with other palaeoproxies, these records provide insights into environmental drivers and eco-evolutionary consequences of reproductive dynamics. The proposed framework opens new avenues for optimising conservation strategies, safeguarding key ecological functions, and improving predictions of future biotic responses.

articles.title: A Stress-Induced Tetragonal Distortion in K2OsCl6 under Pressure
articles.abstract: The structural behaviour of cubic (Fm-3m) K2OsCl6 under compression was investigated to 35.4 GPa using angle-dispersive synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction. Upon increasing pressure, K2OsCl6 undergoes a sequence of structural transformations from the ambient-pressure cubic phase to a tetragonal (P4/mnc) phase above 9.5(3) GPa, followed by a transition to a monoclinic (P21/n) phase beginning at approximately 14.2 GPa. The tetragonal and monoclinic phases coexist over the pressure range 14.2-17.2 GPa, while the monoclinic phase is observed as the sole phase at 17.9 GPa and remains stable up to the maximum pressure investigated. Analysis of the diffraction profiles and unit-cell parameters indicates that the intermediate tetragonal structure is likely associated with stress-induced symmetry lowering rather than a distinct thermodynamic phase. This distortion, which is adequately described by the tetragonal P4/mnc space group, is attributed to non-hydrostatic deviatoric stresses arising from the pressure-transmitting medium. Equation-of-state analysis reveals a pronounced reduction in compressibility across the structural transitions, with the bulk modulus increasing from 26(2) GPa for the cubic phase to 71(3) GPa for the monoclinic phase. The pressure-induced structural sequence is analogous to that reported for related compounds such as K2IrCl6, although the transitions in K2OsCl6 occur at lower pressures. All structural transformations are reversible upon decompression.

articles.title: Ammonia-Hydrogen Phase Equilibria in Planetary Envelopes from First-Principles-Based Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics
articles.abstract: Ammonia and hydrogen are major constituents of planets within and beyond the solar system, yet how they interact in planetary envelopes is poorly known. We perform large-scale two-phase coexistence simulations of the ammonia-hydrogen system from 500 to 4000 K and 0.1 to 100 GPa, driven by machine-learning interatomic potentials trained on density functional theory calculations. From these we map the compositions of coexisting hydrogen-rich and ammonia-rich phases, and the critical curve that separates conditions of complete miscibility from those of phase separation. The critical temperature increases with pressure, from 500 K at 0.1 GPa to 2000 K near 30 GPa, and we find no phase separation at 3000 and 4000 K up to 100 GPa. The slope of the critical curve decreases substantially between 0.3 and 30 GPa, and the curve nearly flattens above about 30 GPa and 2000 K, where molecules begin to give way to atomic species. The coexistence curves are asymmetric with an ammonia-rich critical composition. For the expected envelope compositions, the phase boundary lies close to, and intersects, published thermal profiles of Uranus and Neptune, implying ammonia may be raining out in these planets today. In contrast, in warm sub-Neptunes such as TOI-270 d, ammonia and hydrogen are likely miscible in all proportions. Together with previous studies, our results suggest that silicates, water and ammonia separate from hydrogen in sequence as planets cool, with implications for their compositional, thermal and structural evolution.

articles.title: Challenging Atomistic Foundation Models on Disordered Carbons
articles.abstract: Foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise broad transferability, yet their out-of-domain reliability is hard to establish. Here, we use pure and O/H-containing disordered carbon spanning multiple phases, competing hybridisations and porous frameworks to stress-test six popular foundation MLIPs. We first screen all six on density functional theory (DFT) energy and force errors and binding curves, then subject four to melt-quench-anneal molecular dynamics and evaluate the resulting structural observables. Binding curves and O/H-containing trajectories reveal unphysical extrapolation and dynamical failures that low DFT energy and force errors fail to reveal. Of the models tested, MACE-MH-1 is the most consistently robust, with low DFT errors and stable MD. Despite differing architectures, OMAT-based models share structural biases, highlighting the importance of training coverage. All four models generate structures of nanoporous carbon that reproduce the principal experimental and specialised carbon potential signatures. Incorporating O/H leaves short-range order largely unchanged but shifts pore-size distributions towards larger pores. These results emphasise the need for application-specific validation and extend molecular dynamics modelling of nanoporous carbon towards experimentally realistic structures.

articles.title: Counterexamples to the total-current Hohenberg-Kohn conjecture
articles.abstract: The total-current Hohenberg-Kohn conjecture asserts that the ground-state particle density and total current determine the scalar potential up to an additive constant and the vector potential up to a gauge transformation. We give three counterexamples for two spinless fermions in the physically relevant setting of three spatial dimensions. In each, a Hamiltonian $H^{v,\mathbf{A}}$ has a nondegenerate ground state with identically zero total current but nonzero magnetic field. Complex conjugation then yields a second Hamiltonian $H^{v,-\mathbf{A}}$, with the same scalar potential and interaction, whose ground state has the same density and the same zero current, while the magnetic field is reversed. The first two examples are noninteracting. One is explicit, with a smooth bounded vector potential and a Gaussian density. The other has smooth bounded scalar and vector potentials in the standard potential spaces. The third example has Coulomb repulsion with unit coupling, an isotropic harmonic scalar potential, and Dirac monopole fields of magnetic charge $\pm 1/2$. The monopole example uses vector potentials defined on separate spatial patches, since these fields are not curls of globally defined smooth vector potentials.

articles.title: Coupling Evaporation, Chemical Reactions, and Crystallization: A Population-Balance Framework Applied to Two-Step Perovskite Crystallization
articles.abstract: A limited understanding of how evaporation couples to crystallization pathways hampers control over the formation of solution-processed perovskite photoactive layers. Identifying these mechanisms-and learning how to select and tune them-is essential for achieving the desired crystal morphology and, ultimately, improving solar-cell performance and stability. To investigate crystallization pathways in evaporating thin films, we develop a simple and general zero-dimensional population-balance model that couples evaporation, chemical reactions, and crystallization. We use the model to explore a range of parameters for a solvent-solute system that follows a two-step crystallization pathway: solvent evaporation first induces formation of a crystalline precursor, which subsequently recrystallizes into the final phase. The model predicts the evolution of the film composition during drying and provides quantitative LaMer curves. Based on these results, we introduce a vocabulary of "supply limitations" and "rate limitations" that enables the interpretation of crystallization kinetics in terms of the governing process conditions.

articles.title: Intermolecular Packing and Cooperative Stabilization in Nucleotide Monophosphate Crystals
articles.abstract: We examine the known polymorphs of cytidine 5$^\prime$-monophosphate (CMP) using dispersion-corrected density functional theory. The monoclinic phase is predicted to be the most stable, lying 1.76 and 3.00 kcal/mol per molecular unit below the orthorhombic and triclinic forms, respectively. Monoclinic CMP contains a ribose-based H-bonding motif along the crystallographic $\vec{b}$ direction, comprising alternating intra- and intermolecular interactions, motivating an investigation of cooperative stabilization along this pathway. We employ chain-of-molecules (COM) and chain-of-slabs (COS) models to quantify the direction- and size-dependent stabilization and extend the analysis to the corresponding 5$^\prime$-monophosphates of thymidine, uridine, adenosine, and guanosine. Successive dimer-addition energies reveal the strongest size-dependent cooperative stabilization along the $\vec{b}$ direction, whereas growth along $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}$ exhibits substantially weaker size dependence. Among the nucleotides examined, adenosine 5$^\prime$-monophosphate shows the strongest chain-growth stabilization in the COM model, whereas the uridine variant shows the strongest stabilization in the COS model. Guanosine 5$^\prime$-monophosphate exhibits the weakest response in both models. Minimal-basis iterative stockholder (MBIS) analysis further supports molecular polarization along the growing assemblies. These results demonstrate how nucleobase identity and the surrounding crystal environment modulate direction-dependent cooperative stabilization associated with extended hydrogen-bond networks.

articles.title: Measurement-efficient energy estimator for quantum chemistry of photodynamic materials
articles.abstract: Accurate modelling of chemical reaction rates requires precise correlated energy differences. Quantum computing offers a potential route to their determination, but extracting energies from quantum-prepared states can demand prohibitive sampling. We demonstrate measurement-efficient correlated energy estimation using an electronically challenging H$_2$DBB--Ru model derived from a Ru-functionalized hafnium metal-organic framework relevant to radiodynamic and photodynamic therapies. The mixed estimator combines a quantum-prepared target with sparse multiconfiguration references and recovers ground-state corrections using magnitude-only compute-uncompute measurements. Analytical variance estimates predict 1.6 mHa precision with a few hundred shots, about 100 times fewer than the single-determinant formulation and three orders of magnitude fewer than optimized Hamiltonian-term sampling. With approximate targets, it reaches comparable accuracy using simpler state preparation than direct expectation-value estimation. Emulator and trapped-ion experiments on Quantinuum Helios validate the approach up to (10,10), including a 50-qubit circuit combining AI-assisted state preparation with error detection, providing a measurement-efficient route to correlated energy differences for challenging chemical problems.

articles.title: NIR-probe transient absorption on rubrene microcavities demonstrates no changes to singlet fission by strong coupling
articles.abstract: Strong light-matter coupling has been proposed to control singlet-exciton fission, yet reported effects remain controversial due to the prevalence of cavity-induced optical artifacts in transient absorption measurements. Here, we investigate singlet fission in dielectric microcavities containing rubrene by probing in the near-infrared region, outside the cavity stopband, to eliminate mode-filtering artifacts. Across contrasting cavity quality factors ($Q = 90$ and $1150$) and a range of exciton-photon detunings ($+20$ to $-110$ meV), we find that the underlying kinetics are virtually identical to uncoupled films. Although minor spectral changes occur, transfer matrix simulations reveal these stem purely from mirror interference rather than modified photophysics. Transient electron paramagnetic resonance further confirms that high-spin triplet dynamics remain unperturbed. Together, these findings establish a widely applicable experimental framework for evaluating molecular photophysics in microcavities, revealing that singlet fission remains unaltered in strongly coupled rubrene.

articles.title: Ultrafast Proton-Induced Collective Dynamics Regulated by Water-Mediated Hydrogen-Bond Networks in Liquids
articles.abstract: Photoinduced proton dynamics in liquids couple molecular reactions to nonequilibrium charge transport, yet the role of alkyl C-H sites as proton sources remains poorly understood. Combining optical-pump terahertz-probe spectroscopy with real-time time-dependent density-functional-theory simulations, we investigate ultrafast proton dynamics following strong-field ionization of liquid ethanol and hydroxyl-free ethyl acetate. Isotope-substitution and control experiments support the identification of alkyl C-H groups as the proton source. The released protons induce quasi-free-electron localization on a timescale of hundreds of femtoseconds, manifested as a characteristic V-shaped transient in terahertz absorption. In ethanol-water mixtures, trace water enhances hydrogen-bond-network connectivity and facilitates proton transfer to ethanol O-H sites, suppressing the transient absorption dip. These findings identify photoactivated C-H sites as proton sources in liquids and reveal how hydrogen-bond networks regulate the ensuing proton and electron dynamics, linking local bond cleavage to the ultrafast charge response of the surrounding liquid.

articles.title: Vacuum-Field Squeezing by Molecules in Optical Cavities: An Exact Bound and Linear-Response Theory
articles.abstract: The ground state of a molecule coupled to an optical cavity contains virtual photons, and squeezing of the photonic field has been found in exactly solvable models, perturbation theory, and numerical calculations. Here, two exact sum rules for the field quadratures show that, within the dipole approximation, the vector-potential fluctuations of a linearly polarized mode never exceed their vacuum value in the ground state of any molecule at any coupling strength. Consequently, the field is squeezed whenever the mode couples to a dipole-allowed transition from a nondegenerate ground state, and the cavity-induced ground-state energy shift cannot increase with the cavity frequency at a fixed coupling vector, which is an exact constraint on approximate methods. Moreover, the incoherent photon statistics, which exclude the coherent part of the field, are never sub-Poissonian. At weak coupling, an exact resolvent expression reduces the squeezing and the ratio of the anomalous to the normal photon moment to linear-response properties of the isolated molecule, with the ratio set by a mean excitation energy. Time-dependent density functional theory with CAM-B3LYP and PBE0 reproduces exact and QED coupled-cluster references for both quantities to within 5% at 45 benchmark points. A survey of 29 molecules gives mean excitation energies of 9.5-21 eV at a cavity frequency of 2 eV and shows that the most polarizable molecules squeeze the field the most.

articles.title: Bruce suppresses autophagy-regulated caspase activity and wing tissue growth in Drosophila
articles.abstract: Caspases are cysteine-aspartic proteases that mediate both lethal and non-lethal cellular outcomes, including the promotion of tissue growth. However, the mechanisms underlying the differential regulation of these activities remain unclear. We have previously shown that among the two Drosophila executioner caspases, Dcp-1 and Drice, Dcp-1 promotes tissue growth in a non-lethal manner, independent of canonical apoptotic signaling. Herein, we demonstrated that overexpressed Dcp-1, but not Drice, was activated without canonical apoptosome components. TurboID-based proximity labeling revealed distinct proximal proteomes, among which Sirtuin 1, an Atg8a deacetylase, which promotes autophagy, was specifically required for Dcp-1 activation. Autophagy-related genes, including Bcl-2 family members Debcl and Buffy, are required for Dcp-1 activation. Structure-based prediction using AlphaFold3 further identified Bruce, an autophagy-regulated inhibitor of apoptosis, as a Dcp-1-specific regulator acting outside the apoptosome-mediated pathway. Physiologically, Bruce suppresses wing tissue growth. These findings indicate that non-lethal Dcp-1 activity is governed by the autophagy–Bruce axis, enabling distinct non-lethal functions independent of cell death.

articles.title: Correction: Cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (CIRBP) adjusts clock-gene expression and REM-sleep recovery following sleep deprivation
Syntaxin11 deficiency inhibits CRAC channel priming to suppress cytotoxicity and gene expression in T lymphocytes independent of membrane trafficking
articles.abstract: Mutations in Syntaxin11 (STX11), a Q-SNARE, result in a fatal immune disorder known as familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis 4 (FHLH4) in human patients. A key diagnostic feature of FHLH4 is defective T and natural killer cell cytotoxicity. Here, we show that STX11 directly binds and regulates Orai1, the pore-forming subunit of calcium release-activated calcium (CRAC) channels. CRAC channels enable store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) from the extracellular space and are crucial for granule exocytosis and nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT)-dependent gene expression in activated lymphocytes. STX11 depletion strongly inhibited SOCE, CRAC currents, NFAT activation, interleukin-2 gene expression, and degranulation in FHLH4 patient T lymphocytes and cell lines without affecting membrane trafficking. Remarkably, defects of cytolytic granule exocytosis, as well as interleukin-2 expression, could be reversed by ionomycin in patient T lymphocytes, and a constitutively active, H134S, mutant of Orai1 rescued calcium entry in STX11-depleted cells. Further analyses showed that STX11 ‘primes’ Orai1 for optimal on-site multimeric assembly, which was Stim independent but required for gating. Priming of ion channel pore subunits is, therefore, a primary function of specific SNAREs which may have preceded their role in membrane trafficking and vesicle fusion.
