articles.title: Carbonate intercalation polarizes Ni and Fe centers in NiFe-LDH for ampere-level alkaline oxygen evolution
articles.abstract: Interlayer CO 3 2− polarizes the Ni–O–Fe motif in NiFe-LDH, inducing differentiated electronic responses at the Ni and Fe sites. This site-dependent electronics promote the early formation of Ni 3+ –O and *OOH, enabling ampere-level alkaline OER.

articles.title: A Research Project for Secondary Schools on Urban Plant Ecological Genetics
articles.abstract: Participation in authentic research projects benefits both teachers and students by linking hands‐on field work with experimental biology and quantitative analysis. Plant ecological genetics is especially well suited for classroom integration, but accessible, classroom‐ready outlines are scarce. Arabidopsis thaliana—a wild species in urban environments with a well‐characterized genome and extensive educational resources—provides an ideal model. Here we present a comprehensive, easy‐to‐implement pipeline for secondary‐school–level research‐oriented projects in plant ecological genetics using A. thaliana. The report includes (i) a step‐by‐step experimental workflow for field sampling, phenotypic scoring, and PCR‐sequencing‐based genotyping assays for environment‐sensitive allele monitoring; (ii) classroom‐adapted protocols and quality‐control checks; (iii) background material and a list of concrete, testable research questions; and (iv) downloadable real datasets and analysis templates for guided interpretation. We demonstrate feasibility with pilot field‐survey data from urban school neighborhoods and report outcomes that validate the approach as a proof of concept. Students can learn species identification, formulate hypotheses about ecological adaptation, perform standardized data collection, and apply elementary genetic and statistical analyses—thereby gaining practical laboratory skills and improved scientific literacy. The methods are adaptable to different time frames and resource levels and can be scaled into broader citizen‐science initiatives, allowing classroom findings to contribute meaningfully to ecological genetics research. This project therefore provides a practical bridge between secondary education and place‐based research, fostering engagement with contemporary questions in ecology and evolution.

articles.title: Black‐Tailed Godwits Eat Animal and Plant Material at a Key Non‐Breeding Site at the Overlap of Two Asian Flyways
articles.abstract: Dietary knowledge of migratory birds along their migration routes is fundamental for understanding ecological and evolutionary aspects of bird migration, how migrants select and repeatedly use specific non‐breeding areas, accumulate fuel for migration and breeding, and assess carrying capacity at key sites in the migratory network. Local changes in food availability and foraging habitat have been shown to contribute to population declines in migratory shorebirds. Nevertheless, the diet of many migratory bird populations remains unknown at key migratory sites. We address this knowledge gap for Black‐tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa) by exploring their diet in the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta in the Bay of Bengal, a key non‐breeding site overlapping the Central Asian and East Asian–Australasian flyways. We assessed how benthic prey availability changed during their non‐breeding period based on 600 mud samples collected from 120 foraging locations between October 2018 and March 2019. In mid‐January 2019, we determined godwit diets by analyzing undigested remains of 15 feces and 15 pellets collected from roosting areas, and compared dietary composition with benthic prey availability from samples collected concurrently. Polychaetes and oligochaetes were the most abundant benthic groups in the mud, but we did not find them in the droppings. We observed intra‐seasonal changes in abundance and body size of bivalvia, decapoda, and gastropoda, which were the main animal foods found in droppings and mud samples, and were positively selected by godwits based on availability compared to other benthic prey. We also found plant materials, rice kernels, and rhizomes of Porteresia coarctata, in one‐third of the droppings. This finding extends previous evidence of godwits' herbivory in the East‐Atlantic flyway to Asian flyways. Scaling up our efforts to systematic monitoring could help address conservation questions, such as the impact of shellfish harvesting on the carrying capacity of the world's largest river delta for shorebirds.

articles.title: Corn or Climate? Climate Change Facilitated, but Did Not Initiate, the Northward Range Expansion of the Green Jay in Texas
articles.abstract: Anthropogenic changes are driving global shifts in species distributions. Two highly divergent bird species, the green jay (Cyanocorax yncas) and the blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata), recently hybridized in Texas following range expansions. While the southwestern spread of the blue jay has been attributed to suburban bird‐feeding, the cause of the green jay's > 2° northward expansion over the last 70 years is less clear. Climate change has been proposed as a driver, but concurrent changes in habitat and resource availability—including widespread supplemental feeding of deer—complicate interpretation. We combine ornithological records, eBird observations, climate data, and economic data to investigate the progression of the green jay's range expansion in relation to climate and supplemental feeding. The first records of resident green jays north of southernmost Texas occurred in the 1960s. Sustained northward expansion was detectable from 1980 to 2021 and coincided with reduced severe freeze frequency from 1982 to 1996. Severe winters occurred alongside a reduced probability of green jay detections in newly occupied locations. However, range expansion increased during the period with the coldest average winter in the 95‐year climate record and coincided with growing supplemental feeding. We suggest that winter food supply on widespread hunting ranches and habitat loss drove initial northward colonization by green jays. Subsequent warming may have then relaxed climatic constraints once this novel resource became widespread. This potential interaction between novel resources and climate change highlights that different anthropogenic mechanisms may work together to alter species distributions.

articles.title: Cuticular Barcoding—A Novel Method for Host Identification From Adult Parasitoid Wasps
articles.abstract: Parasitoid wasps are important regulators of their hosts and highly relevant for the resilience of terrestrial ecosystems. However, data on parasitoid‐host interactions are scarce and missing for many parasitoid species as parasitoids are mostly collected as adults without host association and rearing of parasitoids from their hosts can be difficult. Molecular methods can thus help to circumvent this bottleneck. We here present cuticular barcoding, a novel non‐destructive molecular approach to identify parasitoid‐host associations from adult parasitoid wasps. We tested our approach by rearing the parasitoid wasp Lariophagus distinguendus on two beetle species, and washing off remnant host DNA from the wasp cuticle to detect the host species using DNA barcoding. Our results showed a success rate of 49%, detecting the host species in 35 out of 72 samples. Samples containing pooled wasp specimens performed equally well as single wasp specimens, which indicates that single field‐collected wasps are sufficient to identify host associations. Hosts could be detected in wasps that were fixated either through freezing or ethanol, which also supports the application of this method in the field. The primers Jerry/Pat targeting the mitochondrial COI gene performed better than the universal primers LCO/HCO, indicating that more studies testing universal primers are needed to establish this method. This non‐destructive method allows to preserve the sampled wasp as a physical voucher for subsequent morphological identification which will be essential for its usage in situ. Our study presents a novel method that enables detection of parasitoid‐host interactions, and holds significant potential for conservation ecologists, pest managers and evolutionary biologists.

articles.title: FishMitoCleaner: Automated Stop Codon Processing and Quality Control of Fish Mitochondrial Protein‐Coding Sequences
articles.abstract: Vertebrate mitochondrial protein‐coding genes follow a different genetic code, in which TGA encodes tryptophan and a large number of genes terminate with incomplete stop codons completed post‐transcriptionally via polyadenylation. These features are often mishandled when coding sequences (CDS) downloaded from public databases are processed with standard tools, resulting in errors in downstream codon usage and evolution. Here we present FishMitoCleaner, a Python command line tool automating quality control and normalisation of fish mitochondrial CDS sequences in five steps: character validation, internal stop codon scanning, terminal TGA detection, stop codon processing and length normalisation. FishMitoCleaner cleaned 97.6% of input sequences in 22 fish species representing 7 orders and all 13 mitochondrial protein coding genes. Statistical comparison of RSCU values confirmed no bias in codon usage analysis (Welch's t‐test, all p > 0.05). FishMitoCleaner is a Python command that allows researchers in aquatic biology and fisheries science to perform rigorous and reproducible CDS quality control in a single command, and clean sequences ready to be analysed in downstream analyses. FishMitoCleaner is also applicable to mitochondrial CDS data from other vertebrate taxa.

articles.title: Local Adaptation With Gene Flow Has a Polygenic Basis in a Threatened Coastal Songbird
articles.abstract: Species that span heterogenous environments often exhibit local adaptation despite gene flow among populations. In such cases, the maintenance of local adaptation is controlled by several factors, including the strength of selection, migration, assortative mating, and genomic architecture. The song sparrow (Melospiza melodia) is a widespread songbird with diverse subspecies, including the coastally adapted Atlantic song sparrow (M. m. atlantica). Despite extensive gene flow with a generalist subspecies, Atlantic song sparrow populations have been found to maintain their coastally adaptive phenotypes. We produced a new chromosome‐level reference assembly for the species and whole‐genome data to explore the genomic architecture of divergence with gene flow and the genetic basis of adaptation in this subspecies. Adaptation in the Atlantic song sparrow has a polygenic basis, with loci under divergent selection scattered throughout the genome rather than concentrated in low‐recombination linkage blocks. Signatures of fine‐scale population structure, limited genomic differentiation, and divergent selection on a small set of genes suggest a role for natural selection in maintaining this subspecies boundary. Our findings highlight the complex interplay among selection, gene flow, and recombination in shaping adaptation with gene flow and provide insights into the genomic architecture of ecological divergence within a widespread, morphologically diverse species.

articles.title: Plant–Soil Feedbacks May Underlie Competitive Dynamics Between Co‐Occurring Invasive Annual Grasses Bromus tectorum and Ventenata dubia
articles.abstract: Plant communities are shaped by interactions among plants and soil legacies. Plant–soil feedbacks (PSF) may alter invasion dynamics and change plant community species composition. There have been field observations of the invasive annual grass, Ventenata dubia, replacing another invasive annual grass, Bromus tectorum, though previous work has not found evidence of competition that would support these shifts. The goal of this study was to determine if PSF via soil legacies and competition are present between co‐occurring invasive annual grasses B. tectorum and V. dubia, and if so, quantify their effects on interactions with these species. We measured aboveground per capita biomass of these species grown in biculture with three field soils (neutral, B. tectorum, V. dubia) over two experimental Phases in a greenhouse. We evaluated biomass in Phase 1 with field‐conditioned soil, and Phase 2 in soil conditioned from Phase 1. We used generalized linear mixed models to determine the effect of soil origin and plant density on biomass, and non‐linear analysis to quantify competition regression coefficients. The linear analysis showed intraspecific competition negatively impacted both species in both Phases, but by Phase 2 interspecific competition was weakened in conspecific soil, suggesting positive PSF. Intraspecific competition coefficients were always greater than interspecific coefficients from the non‐linear analysis across soil origins. These results are suggestive of a positive PSF which may alter the strength of competition between these species in a biculture. Understanding how PSF influences interactions between these species provides insight into how their invasion dynamics may change over time.

articles.title: Same Genes, Different Wings: Wing Shape Divergence Among Castes in a Social Wasp
articles.abstract: Wings play a central role in shaping dispersal, behavior, and ecological specialization of insects. In social insects, distinct castes with specialized morphologies arise from a shared genome, raising the question of how divergence of traits, such as wings, occurs despite genetic constraints. We investigated genetic constraints and sources of variation in wing shape in the Eastern yellowjacket wasp (Vespula maculifrons), combining geometric morphometrics and quantitative genetic analyses across queens, workers, and males. Landmark‐based Procrustes analyses revealed strong divergence in mean wing shape among castes. Males showed greater wing‐shape variation than queens and workers, consistent with weaker stabilizing selection. Allometric analyses revealed that individual‐level size‐shape relationships are weak across all castes, with no caste showing consistent significant allometry across colonies, indicating that size‐related developmental programs do not strongly couple wing shape to body size. Wing shape also varied significantly among colonies, revealing a substantial colony‐level component of wing‐shape variation that may reflect shared environmental, genetic, and socially mediated developmental influences. Additionally, we found that queens and workers from different patrilineal subfamilies differed in wing shape, demonstrating substantial heritable contributions. Our analyses also revealed limited genetic correlations between worker and queen wing shape components, suggesting that shared genetic architecture would not strongly constrain independent caste evolution of wing morphology. Together, these results show that variation in wing shape in V. maculifrons is shaped by a balance of genetic diversity generated by polyandry, colony‐level environmental variation, including environmental and genetic influences, and caste‐specific selective pressures associated with division of labor. Thus, caste‐specialized wing morphology can evolve in insect societies despite a shared genome and genetic constraints.

articles.title: Fluorine-free chlorinated Hückel-type salt for more sustainable and safer all-solid-state lithium metal batteries
Critical constraints to ecological buffering in a rapidly changing Arctic: A long‐term seabird study
articles.abstract: Drawing on two decades of research in East Greenland, this study shows that little auks, key seabird indicators of Arctic ecosystem health, can adapt to rapid environmental change through behavioural flexibility. However, increasing storms and mercury pollution are pushing resilience to its limits, providing an early warning of broader Arctic disruption. Abstract Long‐term ecological studies testing global change impacts are rare yet essential in the Arctic, a region warming nearly four times faster than the global average. These rapid environmental changes reshape ecosystem functioning across the pan‐Arctic and affect the livelihoods of local communities. Seabirds are widely recognised indicators of environmental change. Identifying species‐specific critical constraints is therefore essential for detecting early warning signals of population decline and ecosystem reorganisation. Little auks (Alle alle), the most abundant Arctic seabirds, are key ecosystem engineers shaping coastal environments through for example food‐web interactions and guano deposition. We present a 20‐year study (2005–2024) of an East Greenland little auk population, combining long‐term demographic monitoring with behavioural, physiological and ecotoxicological data. We quantified fitness‐related traits (adult body condition, overwinter survival and chick growth) alongside potential constraints, including parental foraging effort, trophic ecology, winter distribution, and mercury contamination in adults, eggs and chicks. Over the study period, climate‐driven ocean warming, sea‐ice decline, altered zooplankton communities, and increasing mercury exposure reshaped environmental conditions. Faced with these changes, little auks exhibited marked behavioural and dietary plasticity, allowing them to maintain relatively stable fitness metrics in most years. However, sustained monitoring revealed key constraints that undermine this apparent resilience: (a) Elevated mercury burdens may reduce aerobic diving capacity and thermal tolerance in adults and were associated with reduced reproductive performance. (b) Chick growth was strongly impaired during years with increased summer storm activity, which disrupted adult foraging trips and provisioning rates. Winter storms are also likely to negatively affect adult overwinter survival. Together, these findings show that little auks can partially buffer rapid Arctic change through behavioural flexibility, but multiple interacting climatic and contaminant stressors impose increasing, possibly cumulative constraints on performance. Identifying such critical constraints is crucial for understanding the limits of resilience in wild populations and for improving predictions of ecosystem responses to ongoing climate change.

articles.title: Molecular architecture of Cryptococcus cell walls reveals species-specific chitosan-dependent remodeling
articles.abstract: This study reveals distinct cell-wall organization in two pathogenic Cryptococcus species, revealing that chitosan loss triggers species-specific structural remodeling that may influence host interactions.

articles.title: Solvent heterogeneity regulates assembly pathways in supramolecular polymerization
articles.abstract: Supramolecular polymers often require solvent mixtures for their preparation but their impact on supramolecular polymerization remains poorly understood. Here, the authors demonstrate that solvent heterogeneity biases assembly pathways in supramolecular polymerization, with the extent of this effect determined by monomer structure.

articles.title: From topology to biological meaning: why plant family classification matters beyond systematics
articles.abstract: Conceptual framework for family‐level classification. Summary Plant family names are routinely used to structure comparative analyses, trait databases, floras, conservation assessments, and teaching. Yet, these names are not neutral labels: changing family boundaries changes the units across which biological patterns are compared, summarized, and interpreted. Modern phylogenetic inference resolves evolutionary relationships with increasing confidence, but it does not by itself determine which monophyletic groups should be recognized as families. We argue that this choice should be guided not only by monophyly, but also by diagnosability, biological interpretability, stability, and practical utility. Recent debates around large‐scale consensus classifications show why these criteria must be explicit. Recognizing classification as shared scientific infrastructure means that family delimitation matters not only to systematists, but to all plant scientists who rely on taxonomic units to formulate questions and communicate results.

articles.title: Recent plant photosynthate as a driver of ecological and evolutionary processes
articles.abstract: Timeline of key eco‐evolutionary outcomes arising from belowground allocation of recent plant photosynthate from shoots. Summary Plants rapidly allocate carbon from photosynthesis belowground via root exudates and root‐associated microorganisms. Here we synthesise recent evidence of our understanding of the consequences of this ‘fast’ pathway of recent photosynthate flux for major ecological and evolutionary processes. This rapid input of plant‐derived carbon to soils shapes food webs and drives processes including soil CO2 efflux, nutrient cycling, plant community dynamics, stability of symbioses and evolution of contrasting modes of nutrition, such as parasitism and mycoheterotrophy. We also highlight how seasonality and anthropogenic and natural perturbations likely determine the magnitude and dynamics of this fast pathway across major vegetation types, but these factors remain understudied. Further gaps in understanding include demonstrating causal links between photosynthate flow and key biogeochemical cycling processes and the capture of photosynthate by co‐occurring root‐associated microorganisms.

articles.title: Insights into two modes of TdT action in human V(D)J recombination
articles.abstract: Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is a DNA polymerase expressed in pre-B and pre-T cells that functions in V(D)J recombination to add random nucleotides in a template-independent (TI) mode at junctions between antigen receptor gene segments. However, cellular, biochemical, and structural studies have also revealed a significant, short-length, template-dependent (TD) mode of TdT, in which it takes instructions from a template strand across a double-strand break. Here, we propose that this can occur through an intrachain fold-back synthesis to generate the short inverted repeats at V(D)J recombination junctions observed in early human lymphoid cells and within the adult human antigen receptor repertoire. This duality is also relevant to the functional and structural flexibility observed during the DNA repair process known as nonhomologous DNA end joining (NHEJ).

articles.title: Frustration and topology in the phase behavior of solute-frustrated $q$-clock models
articles.abstract: Frustration can enhance fluctuations and create new and interesting phase behavior. When combined with the ability to host topological defects, frustration can increase the complexity of a system's phase diagram through topological and frustrated topological transitions. To understand the interplay of frustration and topology on phase behavior, we introduce and study solute-frustrated $q$-clock (SF$q$C) models, in which solute sites are added to the $q$-clock model, a lattice model where each spin can take one of $q$ orientations. The $q$-clock model can exhibit spontaneous symmetry breaking and topological transitions, and the interaction between the spins and a solute frustrates the system, in essence by creating a fixed lower bound on the concentration of positive topological defects or vortices. We perform Monte Carlo simulations and develop theoretical descriptions of SF$q$C models with $q=4$ and $q=6$ to understand their phase behavior. We find that these systems exhibit rich phase diagrams that depend on the choice of parameters. In particular, SF$q$C models have a wide range of interesting low-temperature phases, including the presence of strongly frustrated domains and the absence of long-range order. We also find topological effects even at low temperatures; for instance, we find that topological defects can drive crystallization. We anticipate these results to guide the development of materials that take advantage of frustration and topology to tune phase behavior and fluctuations.

articles.title: Exciplex-Facilitated Charge Extraction and Defect Chelation to Improve Inorganic Perovskite Solar Cells
articles.abstract: Rational molecular engineering of the perovskite/hole transport layer interface offers a promising route to simultaneously address inefficient charge extraction, defect-mediated recombination, and lead leakage in CsPbI3–xBrx perovskite solar cells. Herein, we introduce 2,2′-dinitro-9,9′-spirobifluorene (DN-SBF) as an interfacial molecular bridge to tackle these challenges. DN-SBF optimizes energy level alignment, establishes π–π interactions, and forms exciplexes with Spiro-OMeTAD, thereby facilitating interfacial charge transport. Meanwhile, DN-SBF passivates undercoordinated Pb2+ through multiple coordination modes, including robust bidentate chelation formed by adjacent nitro groups, effectively passivating defects and suppressing non-radiative recombination. Importantly, multipoint coordination immobilizes leachable Pb2+, substantially mitigating lead leakage and improving film biocompatibility. As a result, DN-SBF-engineered CsPbI3–xBrx devices achieve a champion power conversion efficiency of 22.40% along with significantly enhanced operational and environmental stability. This work highlights the potential of versatile molecular bridges to concurrently enhance performance, stability, and eco-friendliness, which may contribute to the development of more sustainable perovskite photovoltaics.

articles.title: Data-Driven Flipping Engineering for High Thermal Anisotropy in Janus Two-Dimensional Materials
articles.abstract: The vertical integration of heterogeneous dies in three-dimensional integrated circuits demands materials with extreme thermal anisotropy to dissipate heat in-plane while suppressing cross-plane leakage. Randomly twisted van der Waals stacks can enhance anisotropy, but their stochastic nature lacks precise control. Here, we report flipping engineering in Janus MoSSe stacks, exploiting the intrinsic asymmetry between the S–Mo–Se and Se–Mo–S terminations as a programmable structural degree of freedom orthogonal to twisting. By integrating machine-learned potential molecular dynamics with Bayesian optimization for a 14-layer MoSSe stack, we identify a structure with strongly suppressed effective cross-plane thermal conductivity of 0.082 ± 0.002 W m–1 K–1 at 300 K while maintaining robust in-plane conduction, yielding an anisotropy ratio of about 760 and 35% higher than the crystalline reference. This effect arises from flipping-induced breaking of stacking periodicity, which perturbs midfrequency phonons (2–8 THz) and leads to band splitting and nearly flat, layer-localized modes. These changes reduce the cross-plane propagating channels and thus weaken their contribution to thermal transport, while their impact on in-plane transport dominated by low-frequency acoustic phonons is negligible. Flipping engineering thus provides programmable stacking-sequence strategy and a versatile route for designing anisotropic properties in layered materials.

articles.title: Experimental Design Signatures Emerge from Topic Modeling of Graphene Oxide Literature
articles.abstract: The literature on graphene oxide (GO) comprises hundreds of thousands of publications spanning synthesis, characterization, and applications in diverse domains. Advancing GO materials requires a structured knowledge map derived from systematic mining of this extensive corpus. However, extracting meaningful insights from this vast, heterogeneous, sparse, and unstructured data remains a challenge. To address this challenge, Natural Language Processing techniques, including topic modeling, community discovery, and parameter extraction, are here employed to establish a framework. Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) was applied to the full text of more than 120,000 articles, enabling the identification of eight macro-domains within the GO literature, and neural topic modeling was subsequently employed to characterize the granularity and heterogeneity of these domains. Parameter extraction was performed using Large Language Models (LLMs) on a subset of 8000 full-text articles, with a proto-ontology incorporated into the extraction prompt. Even with a broad prompt, an F1 score of 94% was achieved against manual validation. The extracted parameters were then clustered through community modeling and compared with the LDA-derived topics. At this intermediate resolution of the literature, we demonstrate the application of a recommendation system for relevant parameters according to the material family and application domain. The applicability of the framework at higher resolutions was further demonstrated through the construction of a data set of CO2 adsorption for graphene- and GO-based materials. This data set was subsequently employed in a downstream predictive case study using an Extremely Randomized Trees Regressor, with different training-test splitting strategies evaluated to assess in-domain and out-of-domain generalization at article-level resolution.

articles.title: Nanopore Signatures of High-Molecular-Weight Polysaccharides with Recurring Structural Motifs
articles.abstract: Polysaccharides in nature possess profound biological significance, and their structural complexity renders them of great research value. However, the structural heterogeneity of complex polysaccharides has long posed a great challenge for analysis. Here, a nanopore profiling strategy was developed for polysaccharide characterization. Experimentally, polysaccharides are hydrolyzed into informative fragments, and the distribution of their resulting nanopore events forms a unique profile that serves as a reliable molecular signature. Seven distinct polysaccharides, including xanthan gum, gum arabic, agarose, sodium alginate, gellan gum, heparin, and chondroitin sulfate A, were successfully identified and discriminated. A profile-based machine learning classifier was also developed, which utilizes the overall distribution profile of fragment events as training input, yielding 100% validation accuracy. Further application of the fully constrained least-squares (FCLS) algorithm enabled accurate quantification of polysaccharide mixture composition, allowing for unambiguous analysis of mixtures of polysaccharides in the same assay. Collectively, this work establishes a universal, label-free, and high-resolution framework for decoding the structural complexity of polysaccharides.

articles.title: Cross-species atlas of bacterial RNA 3′ ends reveals termination mechanistic signatures and evolutionary patterns
articles.abstract: Deciphering the generation mechanisms and regulatory roles of bacterial transcript 3' termini requires large-scale 3' terminus data. We repurpose PATHOgenex, an available RNAtag-seq dataset, leveraging RNAtag-seq-specific read patterns associated with 3' termini to generate the "Bacterminome" atlas, a rich resource of species- and condition-dependent transcript 3' termini of 32 bacterial human pathogens grown under 10-12 conditions. Analysis of sequence elements near 3' termini revealed, along with the classical intrinsic terminator, other known and newly detected signatures, highlighting the wealth of termination-associated sequence elements. Intriguingly, orthologous genes with corresponding 3' termini show different termination mechanisms in different bacteria, often matching the dominant mechanism of the respective bacterial species. Analysis of condition-dependent 3' termini revealed some conservation across species, supporting the conjecture that alternative 3' termini can play a role in gene expression regulation. Our resource, available through a user-friendly web server (https://bacterminome.huji.ac.il), provides a platform for studying transcription termination at an unprecedented scope.

articles.title: Molecular triage and isoform protection safeguard ubiquitin chain editing on DNA
articles.abstract: In an accompanying study, we identify the RPA-ZUP1 complex as a ubiquitin chain-editing machine that promotes removal of RPA from ssDNA. Because loss of ZUP1 causes pathological RPA trapping on ssDNA, cells must preserve a functional RPA-ZUP1 pool to sustain RPA turnover. How this homeostasis is achieved is unknown. Here, we show that ZUP1 is subject to ubiquitin-dependent fate control. ZUP1 ubiquitination promotes recruitment of p97/VCP and ATXN3, defining a molecular triage pathway that protects ZUP1 from premature proteasomal degradation. Opposing this, the E3 ligases UBR5 and HUWE1 define a degradative branch that limits ZUP1 abundance, with HUWE1 restricting its accumulation on damaged chromatin. We further show that cells express a naturally occurring ZUP1 isoform resistant to efficient ubiquitination and turnover, suggesting that isoform diversity provides a protected pool of chain-editing activity. Together, these findings define a homeostatic system that preserves ZUP1 while limiting its persistence on damaged chromatin.

articles.title: Sequential TPRX1 and HERVL activation delineates a progression toward the totipotent-like state
articles.abstract: The in vitro induction of 8-cell-like cells (8CLCs) from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) provides a model to study the regulatory principles of totipotency and zygotic genome activation (ZGA). However, the cellular dynamics underlying 8CLC emergence remain poorly understood. Here, we generate a TPRX1-EGFP/HERVL-tdTomato dual-reporter hPSC line to resolve the stepwise acquisition of totipotent-like identity. We show that 8CLC induction follows an ordered trajectory in which TPRX1 activation precedes the emergence of TPRX1+HERVL+ cells, which most closely resemble the in vivo 8-cell embryo transcriptionally. Single-cell transcriptomics and time-resolved flow cytometry further define a continuous transition from the primed state through a TPRX1+ intermediate to the HERVL+ 8CLC state. CRISPRi and RNA-directed perturbations support functional contributions of HERVL elements and HERVL-derived RNA to this transition, while potential locus-dependent mechanisms remain unresolved. Together, these findings establish sequential TPRX1 and HERVL activation as a defining feature of human 8CLC induction.

Mechanistic Insights into the Colloidal Synthesis of Monodisperse CoF2 Nanorods
articles.abstract: Transition metal fluorides (TMFs) are promising conversion-type cathode materials for high-energy lithium–metal batteries owing to their exceptionally high theoretical energy density, making them attractive for demanding applications such as electric aviation. However, their practical implementation is hindered by sluggish conversion kinetics, pronounced voltage hysteresis, and poor electrochemical reversibility. Understanding the structural and chemical evolution of TMFs and the electrode–electrolyte interphase formed during cycling is essential for improving their performance. Monodisperse nanocrystalline TMFs are ideal model systems for high-resolution transmission electron microscopy because their uniform size, morphology, and electron transparency enable representative nanoscale characterization. Here, we investigate a reproducible colloidal synthesis of monodisperse, single-crystalline CoF2 nanorods and elucidate the mechanisms governing their formation to achieve precise control over particle size and aspect ratio. By independently varying reaction time, temperature, precursor composition, and ligand chemistry, we identify the key factors controlling precursor decomposition, burst nucleation, phase selection, and anisotropic crystal growth. These insights provide a transferable framework for the controlled synthesis of a broad range of transition metal fluoride nanocrystals.

articles.title: Atomic-Scale Dynamics of Strain-Driven Sn Segregation in GeSn Alloys
Plasmonic Coupling within Atomically Precise Nanocluster Dimers for Engineering Hot-Carrier Generation and Molecular Activation
articles.abstract: Activating the exceptionally strong N≡N bond remains a fundamental challenge due to the chemical inertness of molecular nitrogen (N2). Plasmonic nanoclusters offer a promising approach by generating localized electromagnetic fields and energetic hot carriers that can drive bond activation under ambient conditions. Here, we combine real-time time-dependent density functional theory with Ehrenfest molecular dynamics to reveal how plasmonic coupling between tetrahedral Ag20 nanoclusters governs N2 activation and dissociation. Systematic variation of the intercluster separation shows that a 6 Å nanogap maximizes near-field enhancement and hot-electron transfer to the adsorbed N2, accompanied by N–N activation. Consequently, N2 dissociation is achieved at incident field strengths as low as 0.5 V Å–1, whereas larger-gap dimers exhibit substantially lower activity. Similarly, isolated N2 remains intact under comparable conditions. These findings establish nanogap engineering as an effective strategy for optimizing plasmon-driven N2 activation and provide design principles for developing efficient plasmonic catalysts.

articles.title: Ultralow-Threshold NIR AgAuSe Colloidal Quantum Dot Laser
articles.abstract: Solution-processable quantum dot (QD) lasers are essential for next-generation integrated photonic circuits, ranging, and optical sensing. However, their practical deployment remains hampered by high lasing thresholds. Here, we report AgAuSe QD lasing with a record-low threshold of 0.01 μJ cm–2 at 900 nm, representing a reduction of more than 4 orders of magnitude compared to those of previous near-infrared (NIR) QD lasing reports. This achievement is enabled by a well-designed twisted-lattice photonic crystal (PhC) nanocavity delivering extreme light confinement with an ultrahigh quality (Q) factor. The extended photon lifetime reduces the required gain volume, enabling lasing from a single-layer self-assembled QD superlattice (SL), which minimizes scattering losses. Crucially, the robust system allows us to push the operational regime to quasi-continuous-wave (q-CW) lasing at room temperature. These results establish a new benchmark for solution-processed NIR QD sources and provide a technologically viable pathway for sustained CW operation.

articles.title: ADAM17 is a broad HIV-1 restriction factor targeted by Nef to restore Env maturation
articles.abstract: Here, the authors show that the cell-surface protein ADAM17 blocks HIV-1 by preventing maturation of the viral envelope protein, while the viral protein Nef counteracts this effect by redirecting ADAM17 out of infected cells.

articles.title: Brassinosteroids improve nitrogen utilization by antagonizing BIN2-mediated SnRK1 activation
articles.abstract: Brassinosteroids are widely used in agriculture, but their modes of action remain incompletely understood. Here, the authors show that brassinosteroids inhibit BIN2, leading to KIN10 degradation and activation of gene expression and nitrogen assimilation enzymes.

articles.title: Breaking water-structure constraints by Hofmeister effects in interfacial polymerization for polyamide membranes
articles.abstract: Hydration critically governs the physicochemical behavior of solutes in both the aqueous bulk and interfacial environments. As typical chaotropic Hofmeister ions, weakly hydrated anions (WHAs) can reshape hydration structures and accumulate at water–hydrophobe interfaces. Notably, WHAs paradoxically suppress the solubility of certain small-molecule monomers in water while enhancing that of chemically analogous polymers. Here, we exploit WHA-mediated Hofmeister hydration control to regulate polyamide-forming interfacial polymerization (IP), using the piperazine (PIP) and trimesoyl chloride (TMC) nanofiltration system as the primary model. Introducing WHAs into the aqueous phase reduces the affinity of amine monomers for water and accelerates partitioning into the reaction front in the oil phase, remarkably reinforcing IP self-limitation. Simultaneously, interfacial WHA enrichment lowers interfacial tension and, together with accelerated amine delivery, potentially intensifies transport-driven interfacial instabilities. WHAs also lower interfacial water availability, attenuating acyl chloride hydrolysis. These synergistic effects yield hollow-ridged polyamide selective layers with reduced thickness and high crosslinking density, delivering enhanced water permeance and salt rejection. Crucially, module-scale fabrication of high-performance membranes demonstrates that WHA-mediated Hofmeister hydration control is directly compatible with established desalination pipelines. Water structures govern the behaviour of solutes across aqueous bulk and interfacial environments. Here the authors use weakly hydrated anions to reshape hydration in the bulk and at interfaces, thereby regulating amine monomer partitioning and interfacial transport while suppressing acyl chloride hydrolysis during polyamide-forming interfacial polymerization.

articles.title: Metabolic reprogramming of macrophage-specific transketolase orchestrates angiogenesis in diabetic wounds
articles.abstract: Diabetes impairs wound healing by disrupting macrophage metabolism and angiogenesis. Here, authors identify macrophage-specific transketolase (TKT) as a metabolic checkpoint and develop a nanozyme hydrogel that restores macrophage TKT to promote vascular repair in diabetic wounds.

articles.title: Nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate hybrid electrolyte for high-voltage lithium batteries via preemptive passivation
articles.abstract: Batteries require safe electrolytes without compromising performance. Here, the authors develop a nonflammable sulfamoyl–carbonate hybrid electrolyte for high-voltage, long-lasting, and safe lithium-ion batteries.

articles.title: Optical-handedness-driven enantioselective synthesis and programmable chirality encoding of covalent organic frameworks
articles.abstract: Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) typically require chiral precursors or catalysts to achieve asymmetry. Here, the authors report the enantioselective synthesis of chemically chiral COFs using circularly polarized light as the sole chiral director.

articles.title: Size-dependent catalysis of Ru nanoparticles for selective reductive amination of PET plastic
articles.abstract: Turning waste plastic into valuable chemicals requires precise control of competing reactions. This study shows that tuning ruthenium particle size enables selective conversion of polyethylene terephthalate into p-xylylenediamine.

articles.title: Spatially resolving isomeric trisaccharides on surfaces with Orbitrap-SIMS
articles.abstract: Structural isomers can be difficult to distinguish and map by mass alone. This study shows that Orbitrap-SIMS can separate and image isomeric sugars directly on surfaces, offering a new route to study complex biomolecules.
